10.1: Will you, then, my soul, never be good and simple and one and naked, more visible than the body which surrounds you? Will you never enjoy an affectionate and contented disposition? Will you never be full and without want of any kind, longing for nothing more, nor desiring anything, either living or lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor yet desiring time in which you will have longer enjoyment, or place, or pleasant climate, or the company of men with whom you may live in harmony? But will you be satisfied with your present condition, and pleased with all that is around you, and will you convince yourself that you have everything, and that it comes from the gods, that everything is well for you, and will be well whatever pleases them, and whatever they give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the good and just and beautiful, which generates and holds together all things, and contains and embraces all things which are dissolved to produce other things like them? Will you never be such that you so live in community with gods and men as neither to find fault with them at all, nor to be condemned by them?
10.2: Observe what your nature requires, so far as you are governed by nature only: then do it and accept it, if your nature, so far as you are a living being, will not be made worse by it. And next you must observe what your nature requires so far as you are a living being. And all this you may allow yourself, if your nature, so far as you are a rational animal, will not be made worse by it. But the rational animal is consequently also a political, that is, a social, animal. Use these rules, then, and trouble yourself about nothing else.
10.3: Everything which happens either happens in such a way as you are formed by nature to bear it, or as you are not formed by nature to bear it. If, then, it happens to you in such a way as you are formed by nature to bear it, do not complain, but bear it as you are formed by nature to bear it. But if it happens in such a way as you are not formed by nature to bear it, do not complain, for it will perish after it has consumed you. Remember, however, that you are formed by nature to bear everything which it depends on your own opinion to make endurable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either in your interest or your duty to do this.
10.4: If a man is mistaken, teach him kindly and show him his error. But if you are not able to, blame yourself, or do not blame even yourself.
10.5: Whatever may happen to you, it was prepared for you from all eternity; and the interweaving of causes was from eternity spinning the thread of your being, and of what happens to it.
10.6: Whether the universe is a concourse of atoms, or nature is a system, let this first be established: that I am a part of the whole which is governed by nature; next, that I am in a way closely related to the parts which are of the same kind as myself. For if I remember this, since I am a part, I shall be discontented with none of the things which are assigned to me out of the whole; for nothing is harmful to the part if it is for the advantage of the whole. For the whole contains nothing which is not for its advantage; and all natures indeed have this common principle, but the nature of the universe has this principle besides, that it cannot be compelled even by any external cause to generate anything harmful to itself. By remembering, then, that I am a part of such a whole, I shall be content with everything that happens. And since I am in a way closely related to the parts which are of the same kind as myself, I shall do nothing unsociable, but I shall rather direct myself to the things which are of the same kind as myself, and I shall turn all my efforts to the common good, and turn them away from the opposite. Now, if these things are done so, life must flow on happily, just as you may observe that the life of a citizen is happy who continues a course of action which is to the advantage of his fellow citizens, and is content with whatever the state may assign to him.
10.7: The parts of the whole—everything, I mean, which is naturally contained in the universe—must of necessity perish; but let this be understood in this sense, that they must undergo change. But if this is naturally both an evil and a necessity for the parts, the whole would not continue to exist in a good condition, the parts being subject to change and made so as to perish in various ways. For did Nature herself set out to do evil to the things which are parts of herself, and to make them subject to evil and bound to fall into evil, or have such results happened without her knowing? Both these suppositions, indeed, are incredible. But if a man should even drop the term Nature, as an active power, and should speak of these things as natural, even then it would be ridiculous to assert that the parts of the whole are by their nature subject to change, and at the same time to be surprised or irritated as if something were happening contrary to nature, especially as things dissolve into those things of which each thing is composed. For there is either a scattering of the elements out of which everything has been compounded, or a change from the solid to the earthy and from the airy to the aerial, so that these parts are taken back into the universal reason, whether this is consumed by fire at certain periods or renewed by eternal changes. And do not imagine that the solid and the airy part have belonged to you from the time of your birth. For all this was added only yesterday and the day before, as one might say, from food and the air breathed in. This, then, which has been added, changes, not what your mother gave birth to. But suppose that what your mother gave birth to binds you very closely to that other part, which has the particular quality of change; this is in fact no objection to what has been said.
10.8: When you have taken on these names—good, modest, truthful, rational, a man of equanimity, and magnanimous—take care that you do not change these names; and if you should lose them, quickly return to them. And remember that the term Rational was meant to signify a discerning attention to every single thing, and freedom from carelessness; and that Equanimity is the willing acceptance of the things which are assigned to you by the common nature; and that Magnanimity is the raising of the intelligent part above the pleasant or painful sensations of the flesh, and above that poor thing called fame, and death, and all such things. If, then, you keep yourself in possession of these names, without desiring to be called by these names by others, you will be another person and will enter on another life. For to go on being what you have been until now, and to be torn to pieces and defiled in such a life, is the character of a very stupid man, and one over-fond of his life, like those half-devoured fighters with wild beasts who, though covered with wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until the following day, though they will be exposed in the same state to the same claws and bites. Therefore fix yourself in the possession of these few names: and if you are able to remain in them, remain as if you had been moved to certain Islands of the Blessed. But if you see that you are falling out of them and not keeping your hold, go courageously into some corner where you will keep them, or even leave life at once, not in passion, but with simplicity and freedom and modesty, after doing this one praiseworthy thing at least in your life, to have gone out of it in this way. In order, however, to remember these names, it will greatly help you if you remember the gods, and that they do not wish to be flattered, but wish all reasoning beings to be made like themselves; and if you remember that what does the work of a fig tree is a fig tree, and that what does the work of a dog is a dog, and that what does the work of a bee is a bee, and that what does the work of a man is a man.
10.9: Mimes, war, astonishment, torpor, slavery will daily wipe out those holy principles of yours. How many things do you imagine without studying nature, and how many do you neglect? But it is your duty so to look at and so to do everything that at the same time the power of dealing with circumstances is perfected, and the contemplative faculty is exercised, and the confidence which comes from the knowledge of each single thing is maintained without being shown, but yet not concealed. For when will you enjoy simplicity, when seriousness, and when the knowledge of every single thing, both what it is in substance, and what place it has in the universe, and how long it is formed to exist, and what things it is made of, and to whom it can belong, and who are able both to give it and take it away?
10.10: A spider is proud when it has caught a fly, and another when he has caught a poor hare, and another when he has taken a little fish in a net, and another when he has taken wild boars, and another when he has taken bears, and another when he has taken Sarmatians. Are these not robbers, if you examine their opinions?
10.11: Acquire the contemplative way of seeing how all things change into one another, and constantly attend to it, and exercise yourself in this part of philosophy. For nothing is so well suited to produce magnanimity. Such a man has put off the body, and as he sees that he must, no one knows how soon, go away from among men and leave everything here, he gives himself up entirely to acting justly in all his actions, and in everything else that happens he resigns himself to the universal nature. But as to what anyone will say or think about him or do against him, he never even thinks of it, being himself content with these two things—with acting justly in what he now does, and being satisfied with what is now assigned to him; and he lays aside all distracting and busy pursuits, and desires nothing else than to complete the straight course through the law, and by completing the straight course to follow God.
10.12: What need is there for suspicious fear, since it is in your power to find out what ought to be done? And if you see clearly, go this way contentedly, without turning back; but if you do not see clearly, stop and take the best advisers. But if any other things oppose you, go on according to your powers with due thought, keeping to what appears to be just. For it is best to reach this object, and if you do fail, let your failure be in attempting this. He who follows reason in all things is both calm and active at the same time, and also cheerful and composed.
10.13:
Ask yourself as soon as you wake from sleep whether it will make any difference to you if another does what is just and right. It will make no difference.

You have not forgotten, I suppose, that those who put on arrogant airs in handing out their praise or blame to others are such as they are in bed and at table; and you have not forgotten what they do, and what they avoid, and what they pursue, and how they steal and how they rob, not with hands and feet, but with their most valuable part, by means of which there is produced, when a man chooses, faithfulness, modesty, truth, law, a good spirit within, that is, happiness?
10.14: To her who gives and takes back all, to nature, the man who is instructed and modest says: Give what you will; take back what you will. And he says this not proudly, but obediently, and well pleased with her.
10.15: Short is the little of life that remains to you. Live as if on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether a man lives there or here, if he lives everywhere in the world as in a state, a political community. Let men see, let them know a real man who lives according to nature. If they cannot endure him, let them kill him. For that is better than to live in that way, as men do.
10.16: No longer talk at all about what kind of man a good man ought to be, but be one.
10.17: Constantly contemplate the whole of time and the whole of substance, and consider that all individual things, as to substance, are a fig seed, and as to time, the turn of a gimlet.
10.18: Look at everything that exists, and observe that it is already dissolving and changing, and as it were decaying or dispersing, or that everything is so made by nature as to die.
10.19: Consider what men are when they are eating, sleeping, procreating, relieving themselves, and so on. Then what kind of men they are when they are domineering and arrogant, or angry and scolding from their high position. But a short time ago, how many they were slaves to, and for what things; and consider what condition they will be in after a little time.
10.20: Whatever the universal nature brings to each thing is for the good of that thing. And it is for its good at the time when nature brings it.
10.21: "The earth loves the shower"; and "the solemn ether loves"; and the universe loves to make whatever is about to be. I say then to the universe that I love as you love. And is this not also what is meant by saying that "this or that loves," that is, tends, "to be produced"?
10.22: Either you live here and have already got used to it, or you are going away, and this was your own will; or you are dying and have done your duty. But besides these things there is nothing. Be cheerful, then.
10.23: Let this always be clear to you, that this piece of land is like any other; and that all things here are the same as things on the top of a mountain, or on the seashore, or wherever you choose to be. For you will find just what Plato says: Living within the walls of a city as in a shepherd's fold on a mountain.
10.24: What is my ruling faculty to me now? And what kind of thing am I now making it? And for what purpose am I now using it? Is it empty of understanding? Is it loosened and torn away from social life? Is it melted into and mixed with the poor flesh so as to move together with it?
10.25: He who runs away from his master is a runaway; but the law is master, and he who breaks the law is a runaway. And he too who is grieved or angry or afraid is dissatisfied because something has been or is or will be of the things which are appointed by him who rules all things, and he is Law, and assigns to every man what is fitting. He, then, who fears or is grieved or is angry is a runaway.
10.26: A man deposits seed in a womb and goes away, and then another cause takes it and works on it, and makes a child. What a thing from such material! Again, the child passes food down through its throat, and then another cause takes it and makes perception and motion, and in short, life and strength and other things; how many, and how strange! Observe, then, the things which are produced in such a hidden way, and see the power, just as we see the power which carries things downwards and upwards, not with the eyes, but still no less plainly.
10.27: Constantly consider how all things, such as they are now, were the same in time past too; and consider that they will be the same again. And place before your eyes entire dramas and stages of the same form, whatever you have learned from your own experience or from older history; for example, the whole court of Hadrianus, and the whole court of Antoninus, and the whole court of Philippus, Alexander, Croesus; for all those were dramas such as we see now, only with different actors.
10.28:
Imagine every man who is grieved at anything or discontented to be like a pig which is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals.

Like this pig, too, is he who on his bed in silence laments the bonds in which we are held. And consider that only to the rational animal is it given to follow willingly what happens; but simply to follow is a necessity imposed on all.
10.29: On the occasion of each single thing that you do, pause and ask yourself if death is a dreadful thing because it deprives you of this.
10.30: When you are offended at any man's fault, immediately turn to yourself and reflect in what similar way you err yourself; for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and the like. For by attending to this you will quickly forget your anger, if this thought is also added, that the man is compelled: for what else could he do? Or, if you are able, take away the compulsion from him.
10.31: When you have seen Satyron the Socratic, think of either Eutyches or Hymen; and when you have seen Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus; and when you have seen Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus; and when you have seen Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus; and when you have looked at yourself, think of any other Caesar; and in the case of everyone do the same. Then let this thought be in your mind: Where, then, are those men? Nowhere, or nobody knows where. For in this way you will continually look at human things as smoke and nothing at all; especially if you reflect at the same time that what has once changed will never exist again in the infinite duration of time. But you—in how brief a space of time is your existence? And why are you not content to pass through this short time in an orderly way? What material and opportunity for your activity are you avoiding? For what else are all these things, except exercises for the reason, when it has viewed carefully, and by examining their nature, the things which happen in life? Persevere, then, until you have made these things your own, as the strengthened stomach makes all things its own, as the blazing fire makes flame and brightness out of everything that is thrown into it.
10.32: Let it not be in any man's power to say truly of you that you are not simple or that you are not good; but let anyone who thinks anything of this kind about you be a liar; and this is entirely in your power. For who is there that can stop you from being good and simple? Only decide to live no longer unless you are such. For neither does reason allow you to live, if you are not such.
10.33: What is it that, with this material, our life, can be done or said in the way most in keeping with reason? For whatever this may be, it is in your power to do it or to say it, and do not make excuses that you are prevented. You will not stop lamenting until your mind is in such a condition that what luxury is to those who enjoy pleasure, such, to you, in the material which is laid before you and presented to you, will be the doing of the things which are in keeping with man's makeup; for a man ought to regard as an enjoyment everything which it is in his power to do according to his own nature. And it is in his power everywhere. Now, a cylinder is not given the power to move everywhere by its own motion, nor is water, nor fire, nor anything else which is governed by nature or an irrational soul, for the things which check them and stand in the way are many. But intelligence and reason are able to go through everything that opposes them, in the way they are formed by nature and as they choose. Place before your eyes this ease with which the reason will be carried through all things, as fire upwards, as a stone downwards, as a cylinder down a slope, and seek for nothing further. For all other obstacles either affect the body only, which is a dead thing; or, except through opinion and the giving way of the reason itself, they do not crush or do any harm of any kind; for if they did, he who felt it would immediately become bad. Now, in the case of all things which have a certain makeup, whatever harm may happen to any of them, that which is so affected becomes worse as a result; but in the same case, a man becomes both better, if one may say so, and more worthy of praise by making right use of these accidents. And finally, remember that nothing harms him who is really a citizen which does not harm the state; nor does anything harm the state which does not harm law, that is, order; and of these things which are called misfortunes not one harms law. What, then, does not harm law does not harm either state or citizen.
10.34:
To him who is steeped in true principles even the briefest precept is enough, and any common precept, to remind him that he should be free from grief and fear. For example:—

“Leaves, some the wind scatters on the ground—
So is the race of men.”

Leaves, too, are your children; and leaves, too, are those who cry out as if they deserved to be believed, and give their praise, or on the contrary curse, or secretly blame and sneer; and leaves, likewise, are those who will receive and pass on a man's fame to later times. For all such things as these "are produced in the season of spring," as the poet says; then the wind casts them down; then the forest produces other leaves in their place. But a brief existence is common to all things, and yet you avoid and pursue all things as if they would be eternal. A little while, and you will close your eyes; and soon another will mourn the one who followed you to your grave.
10.35: The healthy eye ought to see all visible things and not to say, I want green things; for this is the condition of a diseased eye. And healthy hearing and smell ought to be ready to perceive all that can be heard and smelled. And the healthy stomach ought to be, with respect to all food, just as the mill is with respect to all the things which it is made to grind. And so the healthy understanding ought to be prepared for everything which happens; but that which says, Let my dear children live, and let all men praise whatever I may do, is an eye which looks for green things, or teeth which look for soft things.
10.36: There is no man so fortunate that there will not be standing by him when he is dying some who are pleased with what is going to happen. Suppose that he was a good and wise man; will there not be at least someone to say to himself, Let us at last breathe freely, now that we are relieved of this schoolmaster? It is true that he was harsh to none of us, but I sensed that he silently condemns us.—This is what is said of a good man. But in our own case, how many other things are there for which there are many who wish to be rid of us? You will consider this, then, when you are dying, and you will depart more contentedly by reflecting thus: I am going away from such a life, in which even my companions, on whose behalf I have striven so much, prayed, and cared, themselves wish me to depart, hoping perhaps to get some little advantage by it. Why then should a man cling to a longer stay here? Do not, however, for this reason go away less kindly disposed to them, but keeping your own character, and friendly and benevolent and gentle; and on the other hand not as if you were torn away; but just as, when a man dies a quiet death, the poor soul is easily separated from the body, so too ought your departure from men to be, for nature united you to them and joined you with them. But does she now dissolve the union? Well, I am separated as if from relatives, not, however, dragged away resisting, but without compulsion; for this, too, is one of the things according to nature.
10.37: Get into the habit, as far as possible, whenever anything is done by anyone, of asking yourself: For what purpose is this man doing this? But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.
10.38: Remember that what pulls the strings is the thing hidden within: this is the power of persuasion, this is life, this, if one may say so, is man. In contemplating yourself never include the vessel which surrounds you and these instruments which are attached around it. For they are like an axe, differing only in this, that they grow on the body. For indeed there is no more use in these parts without the cause which moves and checks them than in the weaver's shuttle, and the writer's pen, and the driver's whip.
